470.title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12)
470.hook: a servant despised, wounded, bearing others' griefs; Christians see Jesus here, Jewish readers often Israel
470.howItsDone: Christians read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 on Good Friday in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and many Protestant churches, and lines from it are sung in Handel's Messiah and in many Passion hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, called by name, and your line was you are mine. Whose name did you use on purpose? Day four hundred seventy.

A chariot is rolling slowly down the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. In it sits an official of the queen of Ethiopia, her treasurer, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem. He's reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah, the way people read in those days. A man named Philip runs up alongside and hears him. In the King James words of the book of Acts, Philip asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" And the official says, how can I, unless someone guides me? Then he asks the question people have been asking about this passage ever since: "of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?" Today, the passage he was reading.
screen: `A CHARIOT ON THE GAZA ROAD.` → `AN ETHIOPIAN READS ISAIAH.` → `OF WHOM SPEAKETH THE PROPHET?`

segments.voice: Isaiah describes a figure he calls the servant. Not handsome, not impressive; people look away from him. In the King James Bible: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Then the voice in the poem, a we, has a shock of realization. We thought he was being punished by God. We were wrong. "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows." And then: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Stripes are the marks of a whip. The healing comes through his wounds. "All we like sheep have gone astray." He is led like a lamb to the slaughter and does not open his mouth. And yet the poem ends with him lifted up, seeing light. So, the Ethiopian's question. Who is he? Christians, from the beginning, have answered: Jesus. In Acts, Philip starts from this very passage and tells the official about Jesus, and he asks to be baptized in the next water they pass. The New Testament echoes these lines again and again, and many churches read them on Good Friday. Jewish interpreters have most often read the servant as Israel itself, a people suffering among the nations, since Isaiah elsewhere calls Israel my servant; some have read him as the prophet, or a righteous few. Both readings are old, and both are held seriously. And a fact worth knowing: among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a nearly complete copy of Isaiah, made well before Jesus was born, with this chapter in it.
screen: `DESPISED AND REJECTED.` · `WE THOUGHT HE WAS PUNISHED.` · `WOUNDED FOR OUR TRANSGRESSIONS.` · `JESUS, OR ISRAEL?` · then, large: `WITH HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who carries other people's pain. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone like that: a nurse, a caregiver, a parent sitting up with a sick child, a friend everyone calls in a crisis, someone carrying grief that isn't even theirs. Picture their shoulders. Notice how much they hold that nobody sees. Stay with them for a while, without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for the strength they need tonight. The bell holds the time.
Chastisement. What this suffering servant bore so that we could have peace, Isaiah says, with his stripes we are healed.
Your line: by his stripes. Today, lighten one person's load: take a task off a caregiver, sit with someone tired, or carry something heavy for someone else. Day four hundred seventy.

what it means: a poem of a servant, despised and wounded, who bears others' griefs and is lifted up at the end. Christians read Jesus; Jewish readers most often Israel.
what a scholar hears: one of four servant songs in Isaiah 40–55. the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around the second century BC, preserves it almost entire.

471.title: Everyone who thirsts (Isaiah 55:1–11)
471.hook: come, buy without money; my word shall not return empty
471.howItsDone: Isaiah 55 is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic and many Anglican and Lutheran churches, and Protestant preachers often use its opening as an invitation to grace; verse 8 is often turned to in times of confusion or loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chastisement that healed us, and your line was by his stripes. Whose load did you lighten? Day four hundred seventy-one.

A market in an ancient city. Stalls of bread and dates, sacks of grain, jars of wine, goat's milk in skins. And the sellers shouting over each other, the way they still do in markets around the world: over here, best price, come and buy. Now one voice cuts through the noise with an offer nobody else is making. Come and buy, it says. But you don't need money. Bring nothing. Take wine and milk anyway. Free. In a market, that sounds either like a trick or like madness. Isaiah puts it in God's mouth. Today, a sales pitch with no price.
screen: `AN ANCIENT MARKET.` → `EVERY SELLER SHOUTING.` → `ONE VOICE: BRING NO MONEY.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James Bible: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." Ho is a cry for attention, the kind you'd hear across a market. Hey! Over here! Water, then wine and milk: from what keeps you alive to what makes a feast. And the price is nothing. Then God asks a question that still lands: "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?" Why spend your paycheck, your hours, your attention, on things that don't fill you? Listen, God says, and eat what is good. The chapter goes on: seek the Lord while he may be found. And then a line people quote when nothing makes sense: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD." As high as the heavens are above the earth. Then a picture from farming. Rain and snow fall from the sky, and they don't go back up empty. They water the earth, make it sprout, give seed to the sower and bread to the eater. "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void." In the poem, God's word works like rain: it does its work, even before anyone sees it. And the chapter ends in a burst: the mountains and hills break into singing, and all the trees of the field clap their hands. Christians often hear in this chapter the free gift they call grace, offered to everyone. Jewish readers hear God's covenant love, offered again to exiles on their way home.
screen: `HO! A CRY ACROSS THE MARKET.` · `WHY SPEND ON WHAT ISN'T BREAD?` · `MY WAYS ARE NOT YOUR WAYS.` · `THE WORD RETURNS NOT VOID.` · then, large: `WITHOUT MONEY AND WITHOUT PRICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you've been spending on that isn't bread. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day: where did your money go, your time, your attention? Without judging, notice one thing that didn't fill you. Then notice one thing that did, and that cost nothing: a meal with someone, a walk, a moment of quiet, a laugh. Hold that one. Then think of something you could give away today the same way, freely, without price: time, help, a skill, a meal. If you pray, you can give thanks for what came free. The bell holds the time.
Grace. The free gift Christians hear in Isaiah's market cry: come to the waters, buy wine and milk with no money at all, free to all who are thirsty.
Your line: without money, without price. Today, give one thing freely, with no payback expected: your time, your help, a meal, a skill, a ride. Day four hundred seventy-one.

what it means: a market cry offering food and drink for nothing, and a word that, like rain, always does its work.
what a scholar hears: hoy, an attention cry also used in laments. for scholars who mark a Second Isaiah, this chapter closes its poems, ending with a covenant offered to all and the trees clapping.

472.title: Good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1–3)
472.hook: beauty for ashes: the passage Jesus read in Nazareth
472.howItsDone: Churches often read Isaiah 61 and Luke 4 together, and Christians often describe the passage as Jesus's mission statement; it is read at ordinations and in services focused on the poor, the sick and the imprisoned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, everyone who thirsts, the market cry, and your line was without money, without price. What did you give away freely? Day four hundred seventy-two.

A small-town synagogue on the Sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. Joseph's son is back, the one people have been talking about since he started teaching around Galilee. He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds the place he wants, and reads a few lines aloud. Then he rolls it back up, hands it to the attendant, and sits down. The room goes quiet. Luke's Gospel says every eye in the place was fixed on him. Today, the passage Jesus chose to read in his hometown of Nazareth.
screen: `A SABBATH IN NAZARETH.` → `JOSEPH'S SON STANDS.` → `EVERY EYE FIXED ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Isaiah sixty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound." The Hebrew word behind meek also means the poor, the bowed down, the ones with no power. And anointed shares a root with the word messiah. And then the line in your carry, from verse three: "to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness." In Hebrew, beauty for ashes is a little rhyme, pe'er tachat efer. Ashes were what mourners put on their heads. Pe'er was a festive headdress, a garland. The same head that wore ashes now wears a crown. Three trades: ashes for a crown, mourning for oil of gladness, a heavy spirit for a bright cloak. Now back to Nazareth. Jesus reads from this passage, Luke tells us, and then sits down and says: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Luke sets it at the start of Jesus' public work, and Christians often read it as his program: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed. And look closely at where he stops. Isaiah's sentence goes on: to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God. Luke has Jesus stop after the year of the Lord's favor. He rolls up the scroll mid-sentence. Some Christian readers make much of that pause: in their reading, he came announcing favor first.
screen: `ANOINTED: GOOD TIDINGS TO THE POOR.` · `PE'ER TACHAT EFER: A CROWN FOR ASHES.` · `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED.` · `HE STOPS MID-SENTENCE.` · then, large: `BEAUTY FOR ASHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is mourning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone wearing ashes right now, in their own way: a fresh loss, a divorce, a diagnosis, an anniversary of a death. Picture them as they are. Don't hurry them toward the garland. In the book of Job, a mourner sits in the ashes, and his friends sit down with him in silence. Then think of one small thing that could be a bit of oil of gladness for them: a meal, a note, a visit, a memory shared. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Pe'er. The festive garland Isaiah promises in place of ashes, worn by the brokenhearted and the captives: the passage Jesus read aloud in Nazareth.
Your line: beauty for ashes. Today, help one person who is mourning, in one concrete way: bring food, send the note, make the call, or just show up. Day four hundred seventy-two.

what it means: the mourner's ashes are exchanged for a festive crown, grief for gladness, by God's anointed messenger.

473.title: Too young (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
473.hook: I'm only a child, says Jeremiah; before you were born I knew you
473.howItsDone: Jeremiah 1:4–10 is read at ordinations and services of commissioning, and is often given to young people in churches as a reminder that their age doesn't disqualify them from serving God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, good news to the poor, and your line was beauty for ashes. Who did you show up for? Day four hundred seventy-three.

First day at a new job. Everyone else seems to know what they're doing. Someone hands you a task that feels three sizes too big, and the voice in your head is instant: I'm not ready. I'm too new. Somebody older should do this. Now leave Isaiah behind and meet the next prophet. Jeremiah comes from a family of priests in Anathoth, a village in the land of Benjamin. The book says God's word came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah. He's going to spend the rest of his working life, through king after king, telling powerful people what they don't want to hear. And his very first answer to God is that voice. Today, the prophet who said he was too young.
screen: `FIRST DAY. A TASK TOO BIG.` → `I'M NOT READY.` → `JEREMIAH OF ANATHOTH.`

segments.voice: God speaks first, in the King James Bible: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations." Knew, in Hebrew, can mean more than having information: the knowing of close relationship, even of choosing. Sanctified means set apart. Before he had a single skill, before he'd said a word, he was known. And Jeremiah answers: "Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child." The Hebrew word is na'ar. It can mean a boy, or a young man, a teenager or someone in his early twenties. The text never gives his age. What it gives is his answer: too young, not a speaker, not enough. Notice that God doesn't argue. He doesn't say you're older than you think, or you're actually a gifted speaker. He says: "Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak." And then, be not afraid, for I am with you. Then the Lord reaches out and touches Jeremiah's mouth: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth." Like Isaiah's coal, the call goes to the lips, the very place he felt weakest. The answer to I'm not enough isn't you are enough. It's I will be with you. Christians often read this call as a word to anyone who feels too small for what's in front of them, and some hear verse five as a sign that God knows each person before birth.
screen: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE, I KNEW THEE.` · `NA'AR: A BOY, A YOUNG MAN.` · `GOD DOESN'T ARGUE: I AM WITH YOU.` · `WORDS PUT IN HIS MOUTH.` · then, large: `SAY NOT, I AM A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you feel too small for. Settle, and breathe. Name it: a conversation you've been avoiding, a job you don't think you're qualified for, a gift you haven't used, a step you keep saying you'll take someday. Notice the excuse that comes with it. Too young. Too old. Not good with words. Not the type. Then picture the first small step of it, just the first. Not the whole thing. If you pray, you can hold it before God with Jeremiah's honest words: I cannot speak. Then listen. The bell holds the time.
Too young. Jeremiah's first answer to God, I am a child, and God's reply: say not so; I am with you.
Your line: before you were born. Today, do the first small step of the thing you feel too small for. Just the first. Day four hundred seventy-three.

what it means: a young man who felt too young and unskilled, told that God knew him first and would go with him.

474.title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
474.hook: the clay spoils, and the potter makes it again into another vessel
474.howItsDone: Christians often use the image of the potter and the clay in prayer and song, asking God to reshape them, and Jeremiah 18 is read in services focused on repentance and new beginnings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah said he was too young, and your line was before you were born. Did you take the first small step? Day four hundred seventy-four.

A pottery class, week one. The wheel is spinning, a student's hands are wet, and the bowl is rising, actually rising. I'm good at this, she thinks. Then one thumb presses a little too hard, and the whole wall wobbles, folds, and collapses into a lump. But the teacher doesn't sigh and throw it out. She squashes it back into a ball, wets it, slaps it back on the wheel, and says: again. God once sent Jeremiah to watch exactly that. Not to a temple, not to a palace. To a workshop. Today, the potter's house.
screen: `A POTTERY CLASS.` → `THE BOWL COLLAPSES.` → `AGAIN.` → `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The word comes to Jeremiah: get up and go down to the potter's house, and there I'll let you hear my words. In the King James Bible: "Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels." The King James says wheels, plural. Jeremiah stands and watches. And it goes wrong. "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." Marred: spoiled, ruined. And the potter doesn't throw the clay away. He keeps it in his hands and starts again, and makes another vessel, not necessarily the same one. Then God speaks: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel." Now, this can sound frightening: God can do whatever he likes with us. And the next verses do warn: if a nation does evil, its future can change. But they also say the opposite: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, God will relent. The clay's story isn't fixed. That's the hope in it. One more detail. In the very next chapter, God sends Jeremiah to buy a finished clay jar, and smash it in front of the city's leaders. A finished jar can't be reshaped. Soft clay still can. Some Christians hear this as a picture of grace: as long as you're still on the wheel, the potter can start again.
screen: `DOWN TO THE WORKSHOP.` · `THE VESSEL WAS MARRED.` · `HE MADE IT AGAIN, ANOTHER VESSEL.` · `SOFT CLAY CAN STILL CHANGE.` · then, large: `AS THE CLAY IS IN THE POTTER'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of one thing you spoiled. Settle, and breathe. A conversation that went wrong. A project you abandoned. A promise you broke. A relationship you bent out of shape. Picture it as clay that collapsed on the wheel. Notice the sinking feeling. Now notice that the clay is still there. It isn't thrown away. What would it look like to start again, not to make the same thing, but another vessel, maybe a better one? Hold that picture. If you pray, you can place it in the potter's hands. The bell holds the time.
Vessel. What the clay becomes in the potter's hands, spoiled once and remade into another, as long as it's still soft enough to shape.
Your line: the potter starts again. Today, remake one thing you spoiled: the apology, the restart, the second try. Not perfect. Just back on the wheel. Day four hundred seventy-four.

475.title: Seek the city's peace (Jeremiah 29:4–11)
475.hook: to exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you're in
475.howItsDone: Many churches pray each Sunday for their city, nation and leaders, and Jeremiah 29:7 is often cited as the reason; in many synagogues a prayer for the welfare of the government is said on the Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spoiled vessel remade on the wheel, and your line was the potter starts again. What did you put back on the wheel? Day four hundred seventy-five.

A letter arrives in Babylon. It has come hundreds of miles from Jerusalem, carried by royal messengers. The people reading it are exiles: priests, craftsmen, families, taken from home along with King Jeconiah, living now in the capital of the empire that conquered them. And they're restless. Some prophets are telling them not to unpack; in Jerusalem, one has promised it will all be over within two years. The letter is from Jeremiah, back in Jerusalem. Everyone leans in. Surely he'll tell them how to hold on, how to resist, how soon they'll be free. Today, what the letter actually said.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `EXILES, RESTLESS.` → `DON'T UNPACK, SAY SOME.` → `WHAT DID JEREMIAH WRITE?`

segments.voice: Unpack, says Jeremiah. In the King James Bible: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Marry. Have children. Let your children marry. Grow there, don't shrink. And then the line that must have stunned them: "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Pray for Babylon. The city whose army marched you away from home. The word for peace here is shalom, and it means much more than no war. Shalom is wholeness, welfare, everything being as it should: enough food, safe streets, healthy families, right relationships. Seek Babylon's shalom, because your shalom is tied up in it. Jeremiah also warns them not to listen to the prophets promising a quick return. It will be seventy years, he says, a lifetime. Then comes a verse you may have seen on graduation cards and coffee mugs: "For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end." Thoughts of shalom. It's a beautiful promise, and it's worth knowing its first setting: written to a whole community, to be kept through seventy years of exile, most of whom would not live to see the return. It's a promise for the long haul, not the next week. Jewish communities in the centuries since have often prayed for the welfare of the countries they lived in, and many Christians have read this letter as a guide for living faithfully in any place that isn't quite home.
screen: `BUILD HOUSES, PLANT GARDENS.` · `PRAY FOR BABYLON.` · `SHALOM: WHOLENESS, WELFARE.` · `SEVENTY YEARS: A LONG PROMISE.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place where you live now, whether it feels like home or not. Its streets, its schools, its hospital, its traffic, its people who annoy you. Picture its mayor or council, whether or not you voted for them. Then picture one place in it that isn't whole: a closed shop, a shelter, a struggling school, a lonely street. Hold that place gently. Wish it shalom. If you pray, you can pray for your city by name. The bell holds the time.
Shalom. Peace as wholeness and welfare: what Jeremiah told exiles to seek and pray for, even in the city that took them captive.
Your line: pray for your city. Today, do one small thing for the shalom of where you live: pick up litter, shop local, thank a city worker, or learn a neighbor's name. Day four hundred seventy-five.

what it means: a letter telling exiles to settle in, seek their captors' city's shalom, and trust God through a seventy-year wait.
what a scholar hears: the word shalom appears three times in verse seven. the letter answers rival prophets, like Hananiah, who promised a return within two years.

476.title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
476.hook: I will write my law in their hearts
476.howItsDone: Christians hear the new covenant named at communion, in the words over the cup; some also memorize scripture, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in Lent and at services focused on forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah's letter and the word shalom, and your line was pray for your city. What did you do for the place you live? Day four hundred seventy-six.

A few things never need looking up. They're just in you. Your phone number from childhood. The words to a song you haven't heard in twenty years. A grandmother's recipe you make without measuring. The Lord's Prayer, maybe, or a psalm. You don't consult it. You don't need the paper. It comes up out of you, even at three in the morning. That's a very different kind of knowing from a rule posted on a wall. Jeremiah, with Jerusalem's fall drawing near, heard God promise that kind of knowing. Today, the covenant written on the heart.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU KNOW BY HEART.` → `NOT ON PAPER. IN YOU.` → `A DIFFERENT KIND OF KNOWING.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." A covenant is a binding relationship, sealed with promises on both sides, like a marriage more than a contract. The covenant at Sinai was written on stone tablets. And the people, Jeremiah says, broke it, though God had been like a husband to them. So what's new? "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Same God. Same people. Same law: the Hebrew word is torah, teaching. But written in a new place: not on stone, on the heart. And then: "they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." No one will need to teach a neighbor to know the Lord. Even the least. And last: "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." Here, readers differ, and it matters to say it carefully. Jewish readers hear a promise to Israel: the same covenant, renewed and finally taken to heart. Christians hear it fulfilled in Jesus: at the Last Supper he speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes this whole passage. In the King James Bible, those words over the cup read: "This cup is the new testament in my blood." There, testament means covenant. This week we've walked through the servant, the thirsty, pe'er, a prophet too young, the potter, the city's peace, and now: the heart.
screen: `A COVENANT: A BINDING RELATIONSHIP.` · `NOT ON STONE, ON THE HEART.` · `ALL SHALL KNOW ME, THE LEAST TOO.` · `THE CUP: THE NEW TESTAMENT.` · then, large: `I WILL WRITE IT IN THEIR HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start learning one good thing by heart. Settle, and breathe. Choose something short: a verse, a line of a prayer, the psalm you picked to keep this year, or simply today's line, I will write it in their hearts. Say it slowly in your mind. Then again, without looking. Then again, more slowly. Notice which words slip away and which stay. Don't rush. You're not memorizing for a test. You're letting something move from the page into you. If you pray, you can pray the words as you learn them. The bell holds the time.
New covenant. Jeremiah's promise of God's teaching written on the heart, not stone, with sins forgiven and remembered no more.
Your line: on the heart. Today, say your chosen words three more times, at breakfast, at noon, at bedtime, until you don't need to look. Day four hundred seventy-six.

his law written on their hearts.

original.note: Hebrew: a new covenant, from Jeremiah 31:31.

trapdoor: what you thought: new covenant is a Christian term for the New Testament.
what it means: Jeremiah's promise that God's teaching will be written on the heart, every person will know God, and sin will be forgiven.
what a scholar hears: berit chadashah, a new covenant. Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah's whole passage, and the King James renders the cup at the Last Supper the new testament.
